You say everyone is fully endowed with Buddhahood. Please, Master, explain this in detail."
[The Master] said, "One must also know the difference between the inauspicious and the auspicious. The Master said, "Zhaogqing, do you not have a thousand followers here?
Qing said, "It is rather that [each] is fully endowed with the Way; each is fully endowed with the Buddha. The Master said, "How so?
For now, let us discuss how every person is fully endowed with the Way, and every person is fully endowed with the Buddha. Qing said, "If it is thus, then even the Master is only eight hundred."
The Master said, "Zhaoqing, you have spoken thus because you possess the Way. Zhaoqing said, "Up until now, it has been the Master who possessed it;
what more need be said? The Master said, "If it were so, then there would be the capacity of a self.
Zhaoqing said, "Master, not seeing a single dharma is a great fault. The Master said, "What is it that you lose? Zhaoqing said, [nothing].
"It cannot be helped that I must speak of this. The Master said, "To whom would you have me teach it?
Qing said, "What did the Master just say? The Master said, "Have you even grasped it? Qing said, "Tell me more, then, and let us see.
The Master said, "If you were like this, you would be a Buddha with your total capacity fully realized. Qing said, "Even so, it is still not something outside of one's own nature."
The Master said, "Do you understand the preceding, or do you clarify the subsequent? Qing said, "It is so; it is so.
But I do not know how the Master explains 'understanding the preceding' and 'clarifying the subsequent. The Master said, "If it were merely a single part, it would be a flow of true permanence."
From antiquity to the present, what is it right here? Throughout the entirety of the world-systems, it is nothing other than one’s own original substance, eternally thus, with no other cause.
It is called the Buddha-nature of fundamental wisdom; whether hidden or manifest, its application is sovereign.
When one day you are in accord, that day is Buddha-nature; when at once you are in accord, at once is Buddha-nature.
The nature of all phenomena arises solely as a manifestation of the mind. Whatever objects are perceived are nothing other than the seeing-mind itself.
Originally, they are established as the unmoving nature and characteristics; from birth to death, they are fundamentally equal.

A single portion of the Dharmakāya and a single portion of principle and measure are equally luminous, like a royal seal. Not a single phenomenon comes from without, nor does a single phenomenon go forth from within.

It is thus for every person. Every person has self-confidence that they shall become a Buddha; every person has self-confidence that they are fully endowed with this, which is my One True Dharma-realm (Ekasatya-dharmadhātu), wherein there is no other dharma.
According to such reasoning, this is called "a portion of the flowing stream of True Suchness" (tathatā-pravāha).

It is ordinarily understood and comprehended by oneself; yet this is still merely the cause within the cause, clarifying what precedes but not what follows, and in which the vital spark of life has not yet emerged.
This is called a phrase from within death. If one were to deliberate upon it minutely, there would be no end to it.

Such theoretical analysis—wherein a portion of *tathatā* (suchness) enters the initial stage of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*)—is for the time being based on this practice; thus, a portion [of the truth] is fully present within the causal state.

Zhaoqing asked, "Furthermore, how is it? Is there still something, or not? Qing asked again, "There is not a single aspect of nature or characteristics that is not the true, eternal flow of Buddha-nature;
this is called one's own original wisdom, suchness itself, which has never shifted or turned.

When the sharp point of the mind does not reach it, and the phrase that seizes and replaces clarity and darkness is encountered, by what principle or theory should one respond? I beg the Master’s compassion once more. "Son," [the Master replied].

I shall explain it in detail for you. It is essential that those brothers who perform the work at Zhaoqing understand the Buddha-dharma. As for the subtle and great principles of the school, the Master said:
"If one turns aside to clarify the phrase behind the back, the sharp edge of the spiritual faculty does not reach it.

The two parts of the dharma-nature are fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent. Its application is sovereign; it seizes away the ordinary view of True Suchness and manifests the measure of radiant response."

All mental phenomena without exception are collectively stripped away; the vital mechanism of life turns and shifts, no longer resting in the mind-only, the level and real, the single true Dharma-realm.

This is the cause among causes, the phrase within death. Within conditions, one comes to know that there is the nature and characteristics of cause and effect, which are constantly arising and never ceasing—all things are thus.
Only when this occurs can it be called the functioning of the vital mechanism of life. If one does not act in this way—

This is a measure. To know the fruit by means of the cause is a statement that transcends conventional categories. There is not a single dharma that does not arise from compassion giving rise to wisdom;
there is not a single dharma that does not arise from wisdom giving rise to compassion. Furthermore, there is not a single dharma that is not of a dual nature of essence and appearance.
It does not rest upon a mind-state that is level, substantial, or uniform. Today, I have engaged in this theoretical discussion with Zhaoqing; I do not know if it accords with the sages.
"No. "Then how would you do it? Qing asked again. "According to this principle," [the Master] said, "only then can it be called 'clarifying what is before and clarifying what is after.

Two parts constitute the vital energy of life; two parts constitute the capacity that transcends the ordinary. Two parts are the turning and shifting of the sharp edge of life and death, applied with sovereign freedom, leaving no room for host or guest, penetrating both existence and non-existence, neither arising nor ceasing. Two parts are the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); there is not even one more."
If the Dharma were thus, it would not be the simultaneous illumination of compassion and wisdom; nor would it abide within the measure of compassion and wisdom.
Entering the gate of the samādhi of loving-kindness to extensively benefit all beings—what theoretical principle could possibly link this to the words of the ancient masters?
I beg the Master to explain each point clearly for me, so that the assembly of monks may come to know the Master of the Mountain. Together...

At that time, it was like the principle of simultaneously throwing three wooden balls; furthermore, it was so that future brothers in the study of the Way might understand the point where the fundamental principles reside.
He further requested compassion. The Master said, "If the three parts are fully complete in both nature and characteristics."
There is not a single dharma that is not so; there is not a single dharma that is not otherwise. Primordially constant, it has never undergone birth or cessation.

Appearing and disappearing with sovereign ease, it extensively benefits all sentient beings. Complete in its three aspects, it penetrates both past and present, its radiance manifesting or remaining hidden as appropriate.
One does not perceive a single dharma that is not so; one does not perceive a single dharma that is not otherwise. The dharmakāya, sambhogakāya, nirmāṇakāya, and response-bodies are all thus.
They assist the measure of the luminous sages and aid the path of the One Vehicle. Nevertheless, within the *tathatā* dharma-realm, [all these distinctions are ultimately non-dual].

There is neither self nor other; therefore, it is called the nature and characteristics of the single suchness (*eka-tathatā*). It does not abide within the measure of wisdom and compassion, but universally illuminates the gateway of the samādhi of loving-kindness.
It manifests the practice of samādhi within the oceanic assembly of the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*), which is the ancestral style of the ten directions, layer upon layer.
"Have you attained it yet? Are you in accord with the ancient sages yet? Zhaoqing asked. "But how is that so?
What more could be said to attain it? What else could be said to be such? [I] shall now speak a small portion of it; there is no other reason for it.
The Master further said to Zhaoqing, "At all times, you must speak [the truth] all at once. Zhaoqing said, "What more could I possibly say?
The Master said, "Your very way of being is itself speaking all at once. Zhaoqing said, "I dare not. I dare not.
Zhaoqing asked again, "'The mark of the cessation of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words. How then can it be spoken? The Master—
[Qingyuan] said, "The Master speaks to proclaim all dharmas. How is it that they are extinguished? [Yunmen] said, "In that case, you, Master, are one who proclaims all dharmas through words.
[Yunmen] said, "They are all dharmas; they are proclaimed by words. [Qingyuan] said, "Can one still practice them or not?
[Yunmen] said, "There is nothing that cannot be practiced, but how would you say so? [Qingyuan] said, "The mark of the extinction of all dharmas..."
[The Master] said, "It can be expressed in words. The Teacher said, "Yes, yes. Qing said, "Nyo! Nyo! When the Teacher was leaving, he asked, "Where is my staff?

Elder Taoyan said, "It is in [my] hand. The Teacher said, "How did my staff come to be in your hand? Taoyan said, "Take hold of the staff. The Teacher said, "This is not the principle. Elder Zhanyuan said:
Xuedou said, "What harm is there in seizing it? The Master said, "Hūṃ! Hūṃ! The Buddha-dharma is not this principle.
Xingfu asked, "If one is 'responding without a fixed location,' what then? The Master said, "It is not this principle.
Lingzhao said, "Does the Master not want the staff? The Master said, "It is not this principle. Elder Taogong said, "So many..."
None of the people there grasped the Master’s meaning. Not knowing how the Abbot would respond, the Master said, "I intend to take my robes and bowl and travel.
Daoyao asked, "Where will you go? The Master replied, "I am going back to the Prefecture. He added, "My friends, you must proceed with single-minded resolve;
do not merely understand matters in this way, for there will be no end to it. Each of you must take good care of yourselves."
Take heed. [The Master] then raised an example: The Patriarch said, "Perfectly identical to the great void; there is neither lack nor excess.
The Master, however, remarked, "The Great Patriarch only spoke half of it. A monk asked, "What was the meaning of the National Teacher’s three calls to his attendant?
The Master replied, "It was actually the attendant who understood. While the Master was seated, Zhongta and Dizang were standing in attendance. [The Master] then struck Zhongta once.
[The Master] struck him with his staff and said, "As for the name and as for the substance, the stupa has no counterpart. The Master then asked Dizang, "And what about you?
Dizang replied, "This monk deserves a blow; he does not know where it comes from."

In the *Extensive Record* (Guǎnglù) of the Great Master Xuánshā Zōngyì of Fúzhōu, many printing blocks had been in circulation for a long time; consequently, more than thirty blocks had their characters worn away.

[Chìzǔ] therefore visited the Abbot [Zuòyuán] residing in the mountains, and with a shared resolve, they solicited donations to carve new woodblocks to replace them, thereby restoring the work to its complete form. May it...
In this work, which is convenient for those who observe it, the Way exists within direct perception.
Recorded with reverence on a certain day of the auspicious month in the year Wuchou of the Taiding era.
This concludes the lower volume of the Extensive Record of the Great Master Xuansha Zongyi of Fuzhou.

Ascending the hall, he heard a swallow calling. He said, "Profoundly expounding the true reality (*dharmatā*), skillfully preaching the essentials of the Dharma. Thereupon, he descended from the seat.

A monk requested further instruction, saying, "Master, today as you ascended the hall, hearing the swallow call, you addressed the assembly, saying, 'Profoundly expounding the true reality, skillfully preaching the essentials of the Dharma.
I do not yet understand your intention; what was your meaning? The Master asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Go! Who [is it that does not understand]?"
"I believe you. The Master pointed to a lantern and asked a monk, "I call this a lantern; what do you call it? The monk replied, "I also call it a lantern.
The Master said, "Throughout the entire land of Great Tang, there is not a single person who understands the Buddha-dharma.
The Master went to visit Sandou. Sandou asked, "Do not take offense that, having lived on this mountain for so many years, I have no sitting mat. The Master...
[The Master] said, "Everyone has this. Why does the Mountain Master not have it? He [the Master] bowed and said, "Please sit, please sit.
The Master said, "So, it turns out he does have it. When the Master saw Changsheng, he picked up his staff and asked, "Do you see it?
Changsheng said, "I see it. The Master said, "Do men see it? Do women see it? Do monks see it? Do laypeople see it? How do you see it? Changsheng—
Sheng Wudui asked Master Changsheng, "When Vimalakīrti contemplated the Buddha, he saw that the Buddha does not come from the past, does not go to the future, and does not abide in the present.
How do you contemplate him? Changsheng said, "Let me pass; I have a way to speak. The Master said, "I let you pass. Speak!
Changsheng remained silent for a long while. The Master said, "Who will understand this? Changsheng said, "It is a vain labor to strain one's ears."
The Master said, "I knew well that you would go about making your living within the realm of ghosts.
While the Master was at Xuefeng, Xuefeng addressed the assembly, saying, "An ancient said: 'When light and shadow have both vanished, what is it?
Now I ask you, Master: what words should be applied here? The Master said, "Grant me passage; I have a way to speak. Xuefeng said, "I grant you passage. How so?"
[The Master] said, "I, too, shall let the Abbot pass. He then cited the story of how he was spared by the Venerable Elder Mi.
Dongshan said, "A family of generations-long official rank has for a moment fallen into obscurity. The Master said, "A family of generations-long official rank has never fallen into obscurity.
As soon as a newly arrived monk prostrated, the Master said, "It is because of me that you prostrate. He then asked another monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From De[shan]."
Shanlai arrived. The Master asked, "What kind of words or phrases did Deshan usually have? The monk recounted:
"Deshan ascended the hall, picked up his staff, threw it down, and returned to his quarters. The Master said, "That was a deceptive demonstration.

Later, the monk asked Xuangjue, "In what way was it a deceptive demonstration? Xuangjue said, "I ask you, Senior, to demonstrate it first. The monk then demonstrated it. Xuangjue said, "It is not worth it."
He was serving as the groundskeeper when Xuefeng passed away. Acting as the presiding mourner, he gathered the assembly.

While boiling tea, the Master picked up a tea cup before the funeral altar and asked the assembly, "When our late master was alive, we could simply follow his example; but tell me, how would you act now?
If you can speak, the late master has no fault; if you cannot speak, then the fault lies with the late master."
"Is there anyone who can speak to this? He asked this three times, but the assembly remained silent.
The Master then smashed the tea bowl and returned to his quarters. He asked Zhongta, "How do you understand this? Ta replied, "What fault did the former master have?"
The Master then turned his back to the wall. Zhongta then went out. The Master called Zhongta back and asked, "How do you understand this?
Zhongta then turned his back to the wall. The Master then desisted. When the Master saw three newly arrived monks, he struck the drum three times.
He returned to the abbot’s quarters. Once the monk had completed his formal observances, he struck the drum three times and returned to the hall.
A long-resident monk came to inform the Master, saying, "The newcomer has shown disrespect toward the Master’s seat. The Master said, "Have him strike the drum to assemble the community;
I shall examine him. When the assembly had gathered, the newcomer did not come forward. The Master ordered an attendant to go and summon him to the Dharma hall.
The Abbot [was in the hall]. A newly arrived monk gave a light tap on the back of the attendant and said, "The Master calls you.
He then returned to the hall. Later, while staying there for some time, he asked the Master, "Why did you not examine him? The Master replied, "I have already examined him for you.
Xuefeng said to the Master, "A monk once asked me, 'What is the cowherd’s song? I performed a dance and went straight to my quarters. The Master [nodded in agreement].
Yun said, "This old fellow has not yet even touched the ground with his heels. Feng asked, "And what about you?
The Master clapped his hands three times. Because a monk cited the story of Shenhui and the rubble, the Master said, "As expected.
Because a monk cited the story of Yunyan sweeping the floor, the Master said, "If I had seen him at that time, I would have told him, 'This is precisely the second moon. The Master saw the drum.
Shan drew a circle and said, "No one can get out of this. The Master said, "I knew well that you would make your living in the realm of ghosts. Shan asked, "How about you, Preceptor?
The Master said, "No one can get out of this. Shan asked, "Why is it that you can say it, while I cannot? The Master said, "I say..."
[The Master] said, "I have attained it. You cannot say you have. The Master asked Dizang, "The three realms are mind-only. How do you understand this?
He replied, "Do you see the meditation platform, Preceptor? The Master said, "I see it. He said, "Then you do not understand that the three realms are mind-only.
Later, while the Master was attending Xuefeng, Xuefeng pointed to the brazier before him and said, "All the Buddhas of the three periods of time are preaching the Dharma within this very place."
[The Master] turned the Great Dharma Wheel. The Master said, "Lately, the royal decree has become somewhat strict. Xuefeng asked, "How so?
The Master said, "It is not permitted for anyone to snatch goods from the marketplace. One day, Xuefeng was burning fire inside the Sangha Hall and closed both the front and back doors.
He then cried out, "Save me from the fire! Save me from the fire! Everyone came to extinguish the fire, but Feng would not open the door.
The Master threw a piece of firewood through the window, whereupon Feng opened the door. The Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Ruiyan."
The Master asked, "What words or phrases did Ruiyan have? [The monk] replied, "The Master usually calls out, 'Lord! and he himself responds with an assent.

The Master also said, "He was not without a measure of alertness. The Master remarked, "They are all alike in playing with their spirits; they still require a little instruction," and he added further.
"Why do you not remain within it? He replied, "The Master has passed away. The Master asked, "Can he still be called upon to respond now?
The Master asked the hermitage keeper for fire. The keeper said, "The nature of fire is all-pervasive; why do you ask for fire? The Master said:
A slip of the tongue! Xuefeng asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Mount Gui. Xuefeng said, "What words or phrases did he have?
I once asked him, 'What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? and Mount Gui sat in silence. Xuefeng said, "Do you approve of him or not?
The monk said, "I do not approve of him. Xuefeng said, "Mount Gui was an ancient Buddha; you must go there quickly."
He repented. The monk went to the Master’s quarters and recounted the previous conversation. The Master said, "That old fellow on the mountainhead missed the point of the ancients.
The monk asked, "I do not know, Master, what your honorable intention was? The Master said, "Great as he was, Moshan was caught by this monk's question."
[The Master] was completely shattered. Grand Councilor Wang sent someone with a letter to the Master, saying: "I have built a monastery.
There is a senior monk (*upādhyāya*) in your assembly who is capable of receiving disciples; please send one person to take charge of it.
When the Master ascended the hall, he brought up this matter and said: "Let me ask you all: if a person who is utterly intoxicated were to come, how would you receive him? Because of this...
[The Master] cited a verse by Dharma Master Zhao: "The four elements originally have no master; the five aggregates are fundamentally empty.

To bring one’s head to the edge of a white blade is just like cutting the spring breeze. The Master said, "Whether great or small, even when Dharma Master Zhao was about to pass away, he was still speaking in his sleep."
He cited the story of Yangshan planting his spade and said, "If I had been there at that time, I would have kicked the spade over for him.
He then cited how Juzhi would simply raise a single finger whenever he saw a monk ask a question, and the Master said, "If I had been there at that time, I would have snapped that finger off for him.
Finally, he cited the story of Shitou carrying a letter for Master Rang, and the Master said:
The large and small stones were pushed by Master Ryōzan into a pit; even until this day, they cannot be raised.

He then cited the story of National Teacher Lu, who would simply face the wall whenever he saw a monk coming. The Master said, "Had I seen him at that time, I would have struck him five times with my fire-tongs.
He then cited the dialogue regarding the raising of the whisk by Guishan and Xiangyan. The Master said, "It is right here at Xiangyan’s heels."
While he was still at Weidian, the Master ordered a monk to carry a letter up to Xuefeng. When Xuefeng opened it, he saw only three sheets of blank white paper.
He picked them up and asked the monk, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not. Xuefeng said, "Did you not hear it said that 'the gentleman shares the same breeze from a thousand miles away'?
The monk reported this to the Master. The Master said, "The old fellow on the mountain missed his mark, and he does not even know it."
[The monk] asked, "I do not yet understand; what is the Master’s honorable intention? The Master said, "It is still cold in the first month of spring. [The monk] did not know how to respond.
When the Master was at Xuefeng, Xuefeng entered the hall for formal instruction. When the assembly had gathered, a monk bowed and departed with the words, "Take care" (*zhēnzhòng*).
Xuefeng said, "If everyone were like this monk, I would save so much mental effort! The Master remarked, "For the Master to receive people in such a manner is to blind the people of Min."
Zhongyi Chengrenyan asked, "What do you say to this? Fengyun said, "How would you respond? The Master said, "Thirty blows of the staff would be appropriate.
He then cited Fuda Shi, who said, "If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is right here in this very sound of speech.
The Master said, "Big as he was, Fuda Shi recognized only that which is bright and alert. He then cited a monk who, while working outside the gate, saw a snake.
The Master went to see him. Taking up his staff, he struck the head [of the monk] and said, "A snake? A snake? He then cited Changqing’s verse on seizing the opportunity:
"How very wrong! How very wrong! When the curtain is rolled up, one sees the whole world.
If someone asks me what school I understand, I take up my whisk and strike them straight across the mouth. The Master said, "I do not speak in that way. How very wrong! How very wrong!"
"Correct! When the curtain is rolled up, one sees the whole world. If someone asks me which school I understand, I take up my whisk and do not strike.
He ascended the hall and said: "I have studied together with Śākyamuni. A monk asked: "I have heard the Master say, 'I have studied together with Śākyamuni...'"
[The Master] said, "A fellow practitioner. [The monk] asked, "I do not know for certain whom you have taken as your teacher.
The Master said, "Xie Sanlang on the fishing boat. Xuefeng asked, "Which one is the Ascetic Bei? The Master said, "I would never dare to deceive or intimidate others.

Once, while they were working together carrying firewood, the Master said, "All of you rely entirely upon my strength. A monk asked, "If we rely upon the Master's strength, what need is there [for further effort]?"
During a communal work session (*fusshō*), the Master said, "If you do not participate in the communal work, how can you get firewood back?

Later, while they were threshing grain during another communal work session, the Master suddenly fell to the ground and cried out, "O Father! O Father! The assembly of monks all approached him and asked, "Is the Master at ease?"
The Master said, "All you three or four hundred people are beating me right on my belly; how can I possibly find peace and happiness?
He ascended the hall. After a long silence, the entire assembly remarked that the Master was not preaching the Dharma and dispersed all at once. The Master then rebuked them, saying:
Looking at them, they are all exactly the same; not a single one possesses wisdom or insight. As soon as I open my two flaps of skin, they all scramble to seek out words and intellectual conjectures.
They think this is my sincere effort for their sake, yet they remain entirely unaware. Looking at it, how difficult, how truly difficult!
How difficult, how truly difficult!
Ascending the hall, after a long silence, he said: "I have brought you to utter exhaustion for your sake. Do you understand? A monk asked: "What is it like when all is silent and wordless?
The Master said: "Why do you babble in your sleep? The monk pressed further: "I ask the Master for his fundamental teaching.
The Master said: "Why are you so drowsy? The monk said: "I am indeed drowsy; what about you, Master? The Master said: "How can you be so lacking in spirit?"

He recognized [the student’s] pain and itching. He further said, "It is a pity that such great masters and monks, having traveled thousands of miles from afar to reach this place, should depart defeated by nothing more than a drowsy, sleep-talking remark. He asked, "Please, Master, receive me. The Master said:
"I have received you. Will you return? [The monk] asked. "Regarding the ancestral vehicle (zongcheng) from above, how is it to be discussed? The Master said, "Few people listen.
[The monk] asked, "I, a student, ask for a word from the Master regarding the point of intimacy. The Master said, "If you recognize it, then you have attained it.
[The monk] said, "I beg the Venerable One to speak directly. The Master said, "Why do you act as if you were deaf?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "All you practitioners of Chan! You all have traveled from various regions on foot, calling yourselves students of Chan and seekers of the Way.
Is it because there is some extraordinary place to go? Or is it simply that you ask about this and that as you travel west and east?
If there is such a thing, try saying it for me to see; I shall bear witness for you. As for right and wrong, I know them all thoroughly. Do you have anything to say? If not, then..."
To know this is merely to chase after a clod of earth. You have come here; I now ask you: do you all possess eyes?
If you do, then you ought to recognize it right now. Do you understand? If you do not recognize it, you will be called a person who is born blind and deaf.
Is that so? Would you be willing to speak thus? O practitioners of Zen, do not deceive yourselves either.

"Stop! This is your true reality. When have you ever been such a person? All the Buddhas of the ten directions hold you upon the crown of their heads, not daring to place even a single atom of error upon you; they simply say that this matter can only be known by me alone.
Now, as for those who succeed one another, everyone says they inherit from Śākyamuni. I say that Śākyamuni and I are fellow practitioners. You say you are practicing..."
"Who is it? Do you understand? It is not at all easy to know. Is it not only through great awakening that one attains it?

If it were merely a limited measure of what you have awakened to, you would be unable to behold it intimately. Do you recognize this great awakening? It is not a matter of recognizing his mirror-like reflection before a skull.
It is not for you to speak of emptiness or existence, or to speak of this side or that side; there are worldly dharmas."

There is something that is not of the mundane world. You monks, even empty space arises from delusive illusion. If you were to truly realize this with great conviction right now, where would there be anything to speak of?
When there is not even a trace of empty space, where could there be the succession of karma within the three realms or birth through the conditions of parents?
To establish such things as "before" and "after" is, even to say they do not exist, still a deception.
[The Master] said: "How much more so, then, could there be 'knowing'? For a long time you have been traveling on pilgrimage, always saying that there is a matter of awakening.
Now I ask you: in a place such as a steep mountain or a precipitous cliff, utterly remote from human habitation—is there still Buddha-dharma there?"
Can you discern this? If you cannot discern it, you have not yet arrived. I often say:
"Before the face of a deceased monk is precisely the Buddha-nature (bodhi) encountered at every turn; the divine radiance of ten thousand miles is the mark behind the crown.

If one can perceive this, they will undoubtedly transcend the realm of shadows and cast off the conceptual thoughts before their own skulls. If it were not so, who would serve as witness? O worthy one!
I tell you: all the worlds of the ten directions are, from beginning to end, nothing other than your own true human body.
Where else could there be a single dharma capable of covering or obscuring it? Do you know this? Do you believe it? Can you accept and take responsibility for it?
You must exert yourself greatly. Take care. Farewell.
He ascended the hall. After a long silence, he said, "Do you recognize it? Can you discern it? He then returned to his quarters.
Ascending the hall again, after a long silence, he said, "This is how a person of true reality is."
Ascending the hall, after a long silence, he said: "Dharma is present right now. Do you all see it? Ascending the hall again, he said:
"In sum, it is but a single bright pearl. A monk asked: "I have heard the Master say that, in sum, it is a single bright pearl.
I do not recognize it; I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said: "It is the whole body. What more would you have me teach?"
"Who recognizes it? The monk said, "Although it is entirely present, how can one avoid not understanding it? The Master said, "If you wish to understand, simply ask your own eyes.
He asked, "In the midst of perilous and evil paths, what serves as the bridge and ferry? The Master said, "Your eyes serve as the bridge and ferry.
He asked, "What about those who have not yet attained it? The Master said, "Investigate it thoroughly!"

Ascending the hall, he said: "All of you, when you see something dangerous and evil, or see tigers, swords, and blades coming to threaten your bodies and lives, you immediately give rise to boundless fear and terror.
It is just like a worldly painter who paints a depiction of the hells; having finished painting the tigers, swords, and blades, he looks at it intently and yet becomes afraid himself."
It is not another who has wronged you. If you now wish to escape this delusive confusion, simply recognize the adamantine eye.
If you recognize it, there is never a single speck of dust that can manifest before you;
where else could there be tigers, wolves, knives, or swords to frighten and intimidate you? Even the wiles of Śākyamuni himself would be sought in vain.
There is no place for emergence. This is why I say to you: the eye of the śramaṇa grasps the world, encasing heaven and earth without leaking so much as a hair’s breadth.
Where else could there be even a single thing for you? Do you know? To emerge in such a manner—this is liberation.
"How extraordinary this is! Why do you not investigate and grasp it? [The student] asked, "What is the matter within the Gate of the Patriarchs?

The Master said, "Why are you nodding off? [The student] said, "Master, why do you not guide this student? The Master said, "You dull-witted fellow! [The student] asked, "What is the eye of a śramaṇa?
The Master said, "It hits right on your nostrils. He also said, "When I speak to you, it strikes your skull every single moment."
The skull. Its nostrils are worn away. This is because you do not perceive and do not know. Thus it is said: "The skull constantly dries the world;
the nostrils are worn by the touch of the family style. A monk asked, "What is the student’s fundamental matter? The Master said, "This is your own fundamental matter.
[The monk] asked, "When the kalpa-fire blazes forth, burning throughout the trichiliocosm, what becomes of this person?"
The Master said, "A skull. Later, he asked, "What is the Vajrapāṇi? The Master blew once. He asked, "What is nirvāṇa? The Master said, "I will bury you.
He asked, "I do not need the twelve divisions of the teachings; what is the meaning of the Westerner’s coming?
The Master said, "I do not need the twelve divisions of the teachings. He asked, "The ancients all received people with a sidelong glance; I wonder—"
The Master asked, "With what do you receive people? The Teacher said, "I do not receive people by looking at them with my eyes.
[The Master] asked, "Why is it that you cannot speak here? The Teacher said, "Just now I have blocked your mouth; how could you possibly speak? A question was asked: "I have heard an ancient saying:
'Every step taken and every foot placed down is the site of enlightenment. What is the site of enlightenment? The Teacher said, "I will swallow you up."
A monk asked, "Why is it so difficult to see? The Master said, "It is precisely because it is too near.
Ascending the hall, he said: "All of you are sitting within the waters of the great ocean; submerged up to your heads, you stretch out your hands and ask others for water to drink.
Now, a Bodhisattva who studies Prajñā must possess a great vessel and have great wisdom before they can succeed."

If one's faculties are dull, one must simply apply diligent effort, forgetting fatigue day and night; do not merely memorize words and phrases, for when questioned by others, you will have no way to respond.
There is a certain kind of old man sitting on a meditation seat who calls himself a "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra);
when questioned, he merely shakes his body, waves his hands, sticks out his tongue, and stares blankly. Furthermore, there is another kind who simply says:
The Way is brilliant and lucid; this luminous nature of the spirit-mind acts as the sovereign within the field of the five aggregates.
To act as a "good spiritual friend" in such a manner is to greatly deceive people. I now ask you:
if you recognize this brilliance and lucidity as your true self, why is it not brilliant and lucid when you are asleep? If it were [yourself] when you are asleep...
"No. Why is it that when there is this clarity, you still fail to understand? This is called 'mistaking a thief for one's son';

it is the root of birth and death, the conditioned breath of deluded thought. If you wish to recognize this clarity and spiritual awareness, it is only because of the dharmas of the external environment—form, sound, fragrance, and so forth—that discrimination arises, leading you to say, 'This is clarity and spiritual awareness. If..."
There are no external objects. This luminous and conscious awareness of yours is like the fur of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit. O worthy one, where does true reality actually reside?
If you wish to emerge as the sovereign of the field of the five aggregates, you need only recognize the secret vajra-body.
The ancients said to you: "Perfectly complete and all-pervasive, it encompasses the entire realm of dust. Do you see the sun?
All the various mental activities of worldly people—those things they do to nourish their bodies and sustain their lives—are established by receiving its sunlight.
Now, does the essence of the sun itself have many different forms? Is there any place where it does not pervade? If you wish to recognize this adamantine essence, [look here].
It is exactly like this. Right now, the mountains, rivers, and great earth; the lands of the ten directions; form and emptiness, light and darkness;
as well as your own body and mind—none of these fail to be manifestations of the majestic radiance of this perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna*). Why do you not investigate and realize this?
Instead, you follow others toward the realm of ghosts to make your living, deceiving yourself directly. Suddenly, when the lethal environment of impermanence arrives, [what will you do]?
Your eyes are wide open like a tortoise that has just emerged from its shell. Do you understand? There is no peace in the three realms; they are like a burning house.

Furthermore, you are not yet one who has attained true peace and happiness. Your parents allowed you to leave the household life, the donors of the ten directions provide you with food and clothing, and the local deities and dragon spirits protect you—you must possess a sense of shame and gratitude for these kindnesses.

Only now have you attained it. Do not lie stretched out in a row upon the bed. If you are nourished with gruel and rice until you become like a rotting gourd, you will be transformed and buried in the earth.
Your karmic consciousness will be in a state of frantic agitation, with no fundamental basis to rely upon.
As for all those wriggling creatures upon the great earth, I call them "dwelling through kalpas in hell. If you do not realize this now, tomorrow—
When life comes to an end, they will transform and enter the wombs of donkeys and horses; they shall be made to pull plows and drag harrows, bearing iron bits and saddles.
This suffering is truly not easy to endure; one must feel great dread. The causes and conditions of these afflictions and evil karmas will not come to rest for even one or two kalpas;
they will last as long as the Vajra itself. Do you understand? While the monks were standing in attendance, the Master saw something on the ground before him.
He applied white [pigment] to his eyes. Pointing with a staff, he asked a monk, "Do you see? The monk said, "I see.
He asked this three times, and each time the monk replied, "I see. The Master said, "You see, and I see. Why do you say you do not understand?
[Another monk] asked, "What is a seamless stupa? The Master said, "The size of this single seam. Once, while the Master was chopping firewood, he encountered a tiger. A monk said, "Master!"

"Tiger. The Master said, "It is your tiger. Later, when he returned to the monastery, a monk came to seek further instruction. The monk asked, "Master, today you said that upon seeing a tiger, you said, 'It is you.
I do not yet understand your meaning. The Master replied, "In this Sahā world, there are four kinds of most grave matters.
If a person can penetrate them, they will be able to escape the realm of shadows. Question: Regarding the Third Time the Great-Earved Tripiṭaka Master [Encountered the Dragon King].
"Why do you not see the National Teacher? The Master said, "Tell me, did you see him during those two previous times?

The Master sent a message to the attendant Leng Dao, saying, "I have a matter for you to deliberate upon. When Leng Dao went down the mountain to the Master’s quarters and stood in attendance, it was already late at night;
there was no conversation between them. When the wooden board struck to signal the end of the session, the Master called out, "Attendant! Attendant!"
[The monk] replied, "Yes. The Master said, "The board has sounded; go eat your congee. A monk asked, "Why is it that this student cannot speak?
The Master said, "Your mouth is stuffed; how could you possibly speak? This was because a monk had cited Master Xuefeng’s address to the assembly, which said:
"If you have not yet understood, for now enter through Kāśyapa’s gate. At that time, a monk asked Xuefeng, "What is Kāśyapa’s gate? Xuefeng...
[The Master] said, "Only when you do not see even a hair’s breadth [of it] will you have attained it. Later, when the Master heard of this, he remarked, "Meng Babang has gone off in that way again.
A monk asked the Master, "What is the gate of Kāśyapa? The Master said, "Simply enter through the gate of Kāśyapa.
Xuefeng saw a troop of monkeys and said to the Master, "Every person possesses a mirror of antiquity; even this monkey has one."
There was an ancient mirror. The Master asked, "Is there anything that reflects itself? Feng said, "The old monk’s duties as abbot are too burdensome.
Xuefeng said, "When the world is one foot wide, the ancient mirror is one foot wide; when the world is ten feet wide, the ancient mirror is ten feet wide.
The Master pointed to the brazier and asked, "How wide is it? Feng said, "It is as wide as the ancient mirror. The Master said, "Old..."
The feet of the Han [Master] have not yet touched the ground.
The Master ascended the hall and said: "The sun-wheel in the great void is that by which all people are established; the great void is present now.
How is it, everyone, that you cannot see it even though it fills your eyes, nor hear it even though it fills your ears? If you do not realize these two points, then..."
This is a drowsy fellow. If one attains clear penetration, one sits upon both ordinary beings and sages; one sits upon the three realms.
This dream-like, illusory body and mind do not contain even a single thing as small as the point of a needle to serve as a condition or an object of opposition.

Even if all the Buddhas were to appear and manifest infinite supernatural powers and transformations, or were to set forth such a vast web of teachings, they would never manage to touch it by so much as a hair’s breadth. It only assists the beginner.
"Learning is truly the gateway to sincerity and faith. Do you understand? Even the water birds and forest trees know how to uphold the essential principles.
They are most definitive; it is simply that few people listen. This is no small matter. For celestial demons and external paths to do so would be to betray kindness and violate righteousness;

for devas, humans, and those in the six realms of existence to do so would be self-deception and self-delusion. Now, the śramaṇas of today do not realize this matter; instead, they become men who merely dally with shadows."
Floating and sinking within the ocean of birth and death, when will you ever find rest? Fortunately, you possess this vast and great tradition of the ancestral gate, yet you are unable to inherit it;
instead, you seek to act as a sovereign master within the field of the five aggregates. Do you even dream of such a thing?
Over such a vast domain, who could possibly act as a sovereign master? The great earth cannot support it, and empty space cannot contain it. How could...
"This is a small matter. If you wish to penetrate thoroughly, you must attain clear realization right here and now.
I do not instruct you to grasp a single dharma as large as a speck of dust; I do not instruct you to abandon a single dharma even as small as a hair. Do you understand?
At that time, a monk asked, "What is the fundamental principle of the ancestors? The Master remained silent. The monk asked again, and the Master rebuked him. The monk...
Question: By what gate of expedient means can a student be led to enter? The Master said: "Entering is itself the expedient means. A monk asked:
"When a person with a beginner's mind comes, how do you instruct them? The Master said: "From where have you obtained this 'beginner's mind'? A monk asked:
"I am a student newly entering the monastic community; I beg the Master for guidance and support. The Master pointed at him with his staff. The monk said: "I do not understand."
The Master said: "If I were to act for you in such a manner, it would instead result in my demeaning you.

Now, if you can truly accept [the truth] for yourself within your own domain—regardless of whether you have studied or entered the monastic groves—it can be said that you have long trodden the path together with all people, and that you lack nothing compared to the Buddhas of the past.
You are like the waters of the great ocean, which all fish and dragons, from their first birth until old age, swallow and spit out."
In their application, all are entirely equal. Thus it is said: "One who first resolves to attain enlightenment stands shoulder to shoulder with the Buddhas of antiquity.
Yet alas, throughout beginningless kalpas, you have stirred various deluded emotions, which have coalesced into afflictions, like a gravely ill person whose mind is frantic, feverish, and distressed.
Perverted and confused views are entirely devoid of reality; all the various realms perceived at present are likewise so.

Facing your various sense faculties, they all become perverted. The ancients used boundless, wondrous medicines to treat and counteract this, yet even upon reaching the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), they had not attained true awakening (*saṃprajanya*).
From this, one knows that [enlightenment] is no small matter. The ancients reflected on it as if they had lost their parents.
My dear son, it is like brothers today who see one another as if it were all in vain; where else is there anyone who can accomplish this for you?
It is a pity that your time is being wasted in emptiness. Why not investigate it yourself in secret, observing and searching with meticulous care until you reach a point where no effort is required?
Cease all external conditions and depart. Even if the sprout has not yet emerged, the seed still remains.
If you were to take up the strength of my neighbors beating drums and playing with rice and gruel, using this to impulsively cast off birth and death, it would only deceive you for a lifetime;
what benefit would there be? You must know how to grasp the reality as it is. There is nothing more to do. Take care.
Ascending the hall, he said: "I now ask you all: what matter have you accomplished? In what world do you establish yourselves and sustain your lives?
Can you discern this? If you cannot discern it, it is just like pressing on the eyes until flowers appear—your perception of things is immediately erroneous.
Do you know? Right now, before your very eyes, there are mountains, rivers, the great earth, form and emptiness, light and darkness, and all manner of phenomena."
All things are merely the illusory appearances of a frantic labor; they are called inverted views. Now, one who leaves the household life recognizes the mind and penetrates its source;

for this reason, he is called a śramaṇa. Since you have now shaved your head and donned the robes, assuming the appearance of a śramaṇa, you ought to possess the capacity to benefit both yourself and others.
Yet, as I observe you now, you are entirely shrouded in darkness, like a ground smeared with ink.
If you cannot even save yourself, how can you possibly help others? O worthy ones, the matters of the Buddha-dharma involve profound causes and conditions; do not treat them with indifference.
Do not gather together to engage in idle chatter and confused talk, wasting time like children chasing clods of earth. Time is difficult to obtain; it is a great pity for such great men (mahāpuruṣa).
Why do you not examine and investigate what this truly is? As for the ancestral vehicle (mūlagotra) of the Buddhas and patriarchs from of old—what is it?
The lineage of the Buddhas’ Uṣṇīṣas—since you are unable to uphold it, I have therefore used skillful means to exhort you.

Only through the gate of Kāśyapa’s succession can one suddenly transcend; this single gate transcends your ordinary and sagely causes and effects, transcends the wondrously adorned world-ocean of Vairocana, and transcends the expedient gates of Śākyamuni.
From this very moment, throughout eternal kalpas, not a single thing shall be taught.
I have acted as your eyes for you to see. Why do you not investigate and realize this with urgency? It is not necessarily the case that I am saying, "Wait for three or two lifetimes;
only after long accumulating pure karma will you attain it. O worthy one, what is the matter of the *zongcheng* (the core vehicle)?
It cannot be attained merely by applying effort and adorning yourself; nor can it be attained through the power of knowing others' minds or past lives. Do you understand? It is just like this:

Śākyamuni has emerged from his place; he has performed all these various displays and preached the twelve divisions of the teachings, like pouring water from one vessel into another, creating a grand spectacle of Buddhist activity.
Yet, within this gate, not even a single point can be applied; not even the slightest bit of clever artifice will do.
Do you understand? It is like a dream, like talking in one's sleep. A śramaṇa should not emerge from his place.
The various events within a dream are merely perceived by consciousness; do you understand? One who perceives them is a person of great liberation, a person of great penetration.
Therefore, they transcend both the ordinary and the holy, depart from birth and death, leave behind both fruit and cause, and surpass Vairocana.
Transcending Śākyamuni, you are not deceived by the causes and effects of ordinary beings or sages. Nowhere can anyone recognize you; do you understand?
You remain long attached to the net of love within birth and death, and are constrained and carried away by the fruits of your good and evil karma, having no freedom.
Even if you were to refine your body and mind until they are as empty as space, even if you were to reach the wondrous, brilliant, and lucid mind that is serene and unshakable—
This abiding does not transcend the *vijñāna-skandha*. The ancients called it "like a rushing torrent"; because the water flows so swiftly, one is unaware of it and falsely perceives it as tranquil.
Practicing in this manner, one will never reach the end of the realm of saṃsāra; as before, one will again be carried away by the cycle of birth and death.
Therefore, even these practices of impermanence—even the meritorious fruits of the Three Vehicles—are thus to be feared. If there is no Way...
The eye is likewise not ultimate. How could it be like an ordinary person of this world today, who, without expending even a hair’s breadth of effort, suddenly transcends to possess the eye?
Do you understand and save your mental energy? Would you still wish for such a thing? I urge you: I shall stand here now and wait for you to realize it;
I will no longer instruct you to apply further effort or refine your practice. If you do not act thus now, furthermore—
When will it be? Will you finally consent?

The Record of the Abbot details that the true school of the ancient Buddhas constantly manifests in accordance with things; its majestic application shines everywhere, appearing and disappearing as circumstances require.

Serene and open, it illuminates all heights and depths; you are a superior man at the gate of the Way. With the eye of the Path foremost, you have accorded with the fundamental and enlightened the mind—this alone is the ultimate.
The myriad phenomena are of one substance; the ten thousand images share a single source. Vast and boundless, who can discuss limits?

The events of kalpas past are all present before your eyes. Because people of today are distanced by the passage of time, they deviate from the constant nature and, in their deluded minds, cling to [false appearances].

For a long time, this person has turned his back on the True Dharma and failed to meet a virtuous friend or fellow practitioner. He has merely fashioned his own private interpretations; even when engaging in discussion, it all amounts to mere intellectual speculation.

When it comes to investigating the ground of principle, he cannot distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox. Moreover, throughout his life, he has never sought out the ancient sages and masters of the past.
Furthermore, he knows his own time and nature, yet he restrains himself and yields credit to others, dwelling in mountain caves and stone chambers. Above...
Deyun, if your mind still harbors the measure of the holy, you have merely fallen into the dust of dharmas; if your own views are not yet forgotten, it will still result in leakage.

You cannot say that by observing fasts and precepts, sitting long without lying down, stilling thoughts to contemplate emptiness, or concentrating the spirit to enter meditative absorption, you shall immediately depart [from birth and death].

What connection is there between such things and liberation? Even the non-Buddhist practitioners of the Western Heaven can enter the samādhi of eighty thousand kalpas, concentrating their spirits in silence.
Tranquility. Closing the eyes and hiding the pupils, extinguishing the mind and annihilating wisdom—even when the kalpas have just ended, one cannot avoid the cycle of saṃsāra.
This is because the eye of the Way is not clear and the root-source of birth and death has not been severed. Now, those who have left the home-life are not like this;

they must not be equated with the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). They must be truly enlightened and penetrating, possessing great knowledge and vision, able to travel in the same carriage as the Buddha, and dwell in stillness.
Illuminating forgetfulness and knowing, it emptily contains the myriad phenomena. Right now, where is there that is not you?
Where is there that is not clear? Where is there that is not manifest? Why do you not understand it in this way? If you lack this ground, [you will never attain it].
During these times, what can one do about the many leaking thoughts? They all result in nothing but falsehood. Which of these, then, is that place where you have gained strength throughout your life?
If you have not yet realized the truth as it is, you must truly act with urgency. During these times, forget eating and lose sleep;

treat it as if your head were on fire, as if you had lost your very life. Only by clarifying the mind, investigating the principle, relinquishing idle conditions, and bringing the mental consciousness to rest will you finally [attain realization].
There is a portion of mutual affinity. If it were not so, tomorrow morning or the next day, everything would be carried away by the discriminating intellect;
what freedom would there be? Now, however, they are not like those insentient things that proclaim clearly:
earth, wood, stone, and pebbles preach the Dharma with utmost truthfulness. It is simply that few people listen. If one hears this teaching, only then can one [truly understand].
Consider this: if one encounters a person who hears the insentient preaching the Dharma, how will they discuss it? Try to say something!
One cannot say there is no speaking and no discourse; nor can one say that, without being asked, he speaks of his own accord to extol the path he practices.
The youth Sudhana visited one hundred and twenty teachers; finally, upon seeing Maitreya, he entered the gate in the mere twinkling of an eye.
After Sudhana had entered the gate, the door closed of its own accord.

Within the multi-storied pavilion, he beheld hundreds of thousands of Buddhas undergoing the process of casting off and assuming bodies throughout their past lives—all those spiritual friends whom he had visited.
The manifested realms appeared simultaneously within the pavilions, and Maitreya served as their witness; thus, Sudhana’s doubts were instantly stilled.
Generally speaking, beneath the three rafters of a humble dwelling, one must possess this true realization before one may engage in discussion.
Thus, within the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence, one is identical to the pure lands of all Buddhas; what further fear can there be regarding birth and death?
Furthermore, by whom has it been known that all the teachings spoken by others lack any substantial reality?

Even at the assembly on Vulture Peak, when Kāśyapa heard [the Buddha] in person, it was like painting the moon. An ancient worthy said: "Do not deliberate upon good or evil"—this is likewise like pointing at the moon. It is thus.

As for the stages and positions of the three vehicles, the dharma-body of liberation, bodhi, nirvana, noble wisdom, and the fruits of sainthood—all are like flowers in the sky or the horns of a rabbit.
Not having seen the Way, one returns to observe the world as if it were a dream; such are the conditioned mental dharmas.
One cannot rely on such things. As months turn to years, they utterly fail to provide benefit. This is simply because you have abandoned the root to pursue the branches;

you loathe ordinary sentiments and take pleasure in the Holy Path, forming such views and understandings that do not transcend the limitations of others. You cast off the five aggregates yet still cannot leave them behind.
Have you not heard the Way taught: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are laws of arising and ceasing"? You merely intend to move forward, but how can you succeed?
If you can understand this, you may know it; if you have not yet grasped it, you must know that these are all merely the methods of empty-headed people.
Only those endowed with great capacity (*mahā-indriya*) can attain clear realization. You must penetrate this in this very life; it will be the same for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
As the ancient masters said: "Exert yourself now to bring this to completion; who can endure receiving further calamities through successive kalpas? I have thus written this in my study.
Disciple. Adieu. At the request of King Dae-wang, Xuefeng and Xuansha were invited into the inner palace to discuss the Buddha’s Heart-Seal.
In this record, the Great King questioned the two Chan masters regarding the secret Heart-Seal transmitted by all Buddhas and Bodhidharma; he requested the Master’s definitive [instruction].
This is the true teaching. Furthermore, since the time of the patriarchs and Buddhas, what cause and effect have they ultimately cultivated to attain Buddhahood?
Feng said, "One must see one's nature before one can attain Buddhahood. The King asked, "What is meant by seeing one's nature? Feng replied, "It is seeing one's own original nature."
The King asked, "Does it have a form? Feng said, "One sees one's own original nature; there is nothing to be seen.

This is a teaching difficult to believe, transmitted by hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. The King asked, "Can it be attained? Feng said, "If one were to praise this matter," [the King would not understand].

Even if one were to speak throughout the entire earth, one could never exhaust it. If Daruma had transmitted it personally, it would have been but a single word, which immediately transforms the ordinary person into a sage;
this is no small matter. To realize it is in a single instant; not to realize it is for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Great King, within the Great Canon of all sutras and treatises—however many thousands or tens of thousands of types there may be—they all concern but the One Mind. From patriarch to patriarch, it has been transmitted as one.
"Mind. However, for Your Majesty, this mountain monk shall not hastily point out the true nature of this matter.
Your Majesty, because of this matter, each of my followers numbers in the thousands and hundreds;
yet for twenty or thirty years, we have applied this matter in secret, and not even one or two persons among them has been able to take it up. Moreover, this Dharma-gate is that of the past..."

The Buddhas transmit this Dharma from one person to another alone. How much more so now, when Your Majesty, as a secular sovereign, daily adjudicates the affairs of the myriad people and the mountains and rivers?
If you harbor deluded thoughts, how could you ever encounter this true Dharma-gate?
I pray that Your Majesty will act as the master of the Buddha-Dharma and, through the tip of your pen, rescue and protect all living beings. Is this not a matter of great importance? Great!
Upon hearing this exhortation, the King’s joy redoubled. He further questioned the two masters: "I now intend to build monasteries, cultivate merit, practice giving, and ordain monks.
By refraining from all evil and performing all good, as it is said, will I still attain Buddhahood? Xuan Sha replied, "One cannot attain Buddhahood through such means;
for any mind that involves deliberate effort is entirely within the cycle of saṃsāra. The Great King asked, "Then can one attain it?"
"What is the retribution? The Master said, "One obtains the retribution of rebirth in heaven; one obtains the retribution of merit and longevity. The King asked, "Ultimately, what happens?
The Master said, "When merit is exhausted, one falls. The King asked, "Where does one fall? The Master said, "When merit is exhausted, one falls back into the retribution of longevity.

"The Buddha’s scriptures record this in detail," [the Master continued]. For a short while, the Great King remained silent. Then the two masters said to the Great King, "The mind itself is the Buddha; seeing the nature is..."
The King asked, "What constitutes the Way? What practice should one perform? The Master replied, "The sutras state:
'The ocean of all karmic obstructions arises entirely from deluded thoughts. If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true mark.

I pray that Your Majesty recognize this true mark, and you will naturally become a Buddha. The King rose, prostrated before the two masters, and said, "Your saving me from the matter of birth and death is a great kindness."
The Master said: "For now, let me explain the names of True Suchness (Tathatā) for Your Majesty.
First is called Buddha-nature; second, True Suchness; third, the Mysterious Ultimate; fourth, the Pure Dharma-body Realm; fifth, the Spiritual Terrace;
sixth, the Essential Spirit; seventh, the Infant; eighth, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom; ninth, the School of Emptiness; tenth, the Ultimate Meaning; eleventh—"
It is called the "Pure White Consciousness. This is the name for the One Mind; within it, the Buddhas of the three periods and the twelve divisions of the scriptures are all present.
Great King, your original nature is inherently complete and requires no seeking. You must urgently save yourself; no one else can act on your behalf.
This mountain monk cannot save you, Great King. I cherish all sentient beings as if they were my own infants, yet when circumstances arise...

One immediately delivers sentient beings through skillful means. If one is to become a Buddha, one must first deliver oneself. Once one has awakened to the single nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), there is no need for many words.
If Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have not yet realized the empty and quiescent true source, they must rely on verbal teachings to transform others.
If one realizes the true source, one accords with the Way through wordlessness. The Way is fundamentally without words or speech; the Buddha’s words were originally without merit.
This is the realization of the Way through its application. Furthermore, it is said: "Moreover, this mountain monk has been invited by Your Majesty to reside at the mountain gate.

Having no choice in the matter, I shall preach the Dharma for the King as a way of repaying his kindness. When this mountain monk preaches the Dharma, it is like a great rain falling, universally moistening all at once according to the power of their merit.
Yet for sentient beings with meager merit who do not believe in the Mahāyāna, it is like rain falling upon withered wood or scorched seeds."
"The Icchantika has no faith," said the mountain monk. "I pray that Your Majesty simply contemplate the fundamental nature within your own person.

If you see it clearly, everything will naturally be understood. That there is flourishing and decline, arising and ceasing, is the teaching of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Now, this "teaching" is that by which the Dharma is clarified;
yet, without relying upon the teaching, one cannot transmit the Dharma. Thus, the flourishing and decline of the teaching are like the flourishing and decline of the Dharma itself.
After the teaching has endured for a long time, it cannot avoid becoming corrupt. If this corruption is not remedied, the teaching will decline. This is why, in the world—

There was a great man who rectified abuses and established the teachings, transmitting them to ordinary people of future generations with vast resolve—teachings that do not involve the vicissitudes of prosperity and decline, nor of birth and extinction.
Now, the emergence of abuses within the teachings is like the occurrence of illness within the human body.
Generally speaking, although the human body may fall ill even in its prime, those approaching old age are especially prone to sickness.
It is so. When disease afflicts the trees of a forest, it may occur even in a single tree; yet within a great forest, there will inevitably be many diseased branches.
In the past, outside of the Three Vehicles, Śākyamuni Tathāgata separately transmitted the life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to Mahākāśyapa.
Kāśyapa transmitted it to Ānanda, and thereafter it was passed down through successive generations from Kāśyapa for twenty-eight [generations].
The lineage was transmitted down to the Great Master Bodhidharma. Bodhidharma traveled and taught throughout the Eastern Land, transmitting it to Huike;
Huike transmitted it to Sengcan; Sengcan transmitted it to Daoxin; Daoxin transmitted it to Hongren; and Hongren transmitted it to Dajian.
These are known as the twenty-eight patriarchs of India and the six patriarchs of the Eastern Land, all of whom transmitted the teaching from one person to another.
It is so. Although there may have been occasional divergent branches in the interim, as far as the transmission of the robe and the Dharma is concerned, it has been singular and without duality.
At this time, it was like the prime of life: the complexion was radiant, the hair was black, the vital energy was complete, and disease could not invade.
It reached the time of Great Mirror (Huineng), however, when the robe and bowl became a cause for contention; he ceased the transmission of the robe and transmitted only the Dharma universally.
As for the transmission: those who have maintained and upheld its Dharma are as dense as a forest.
Yet, that which has been transmitted down to the present day consists of two gateways of nectar: Qingyuan and Nanyue. Qingyuan transmitted it to Shitou, whose school was followed in Hunan;
Nanyue transmitted it to Mazu, whose school was followed in Jiangxi. Furthermore, Shitou widely transmitted it to Tianhuang Wu.
Yaoshan Yan and others, as well as Mazu’s further transmission to Baizhang Hai and Nanquan Puyuan,
and so on down to one hundred and thirty-seven people— since that time, their descendants and grand-nephews have formed branches and lineages throughout Jiangxi and Hunan.
Everywhere they went, the discourse on Chan was vast and expansive, like a hundred rivers rushing together, like a thousand forests competing in growth.
Within this flourishing, it was impossible to avoid the emergence of turbulent currents and diseased branches;
thus, the Chan school gradually reached its twilight years. This was precisely why the maladies of Chan arose.

At that time, there appeared the Great Master Xuan Sha Zongyi, who transmitted the secret dharma-gates of Deshan and Shitou and possessed a penetrating vision into the hearts, livers, and five viscera of Chan practitioners.
Applying acupuncture and moxibustion according to the specific ailment is like the physician from Qin and Yue drinking from the water of the Upper Pond;
he could look at people across a wall and see clearly through their five viscera and internal blockages, thereby exhausting the source of the disease and raising those who were on the brink of death.
Thus, masters such as Zhaoqing Da Shi of his time established their teachings in a single region and were surrounded by thousands of followers. This was just as one approaches a teacher...

If one seeks further instruction, the rest may be understood. His discourses delivered from the high seat were compiled by his disciples into the *Dàlù* (Great Record) and *Xiǎolù* (Small Record), yet these records have long been lost.

It was not until the Ming dynasty that figures such as the layman Shānlín and the Chan Master Yúnmén Rán recovered fragments of the Great Master’s teachings on dharma from within the *Wǔdēng Huìyuán*, the *Chuándēng Lù*, and other biographical collections.
This work is titled the *Xuansha Yulu* (Recorded Sayings of Xuansha). To savor its flavor is like tasting the saltiness of the ocean that reaches the heavens and bathes the sun within a single drop;
it serves merely to satisfy the longing of Zen practitioners. Fortunately, a copy was transmitted to the room of a monk at Taiping Mountain’s Dazhong Chan Temple in Shimotsuke Province in this land.
It was compiled by his disciple Zhuyan in the third year of the Guanghua era of the Tang dynasty. [Song Dynasty...]
Sun Jue, Right Attendant Censor and Military Governor of Fuzhou, commissioned the monk of Xuansha to carve woodblocks so that this work might be circulated as printed editions;
however, the presiding monk kept them jealously secret, such that they could not be seen by the world.
Consequently, when I was formerly residing at Wansong Mountain, I requested of the Abbot, Chan Master Rongfeng, that he would lend me his [copy].

Through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he transcribed this Song-dynasty carved-print edition from within the Great Central Chamber and had it carved into woodblocks for the world, thereby sowing the seeds of Prajñā throughout the land.

Yungfeng also feared that this copy might have no counterpart and would perish within the belly of a woodworm, thus obstructing its life through despair; yet his wish was not fulfilled. Recently, however, Yungfeng has received...
Regarding the national mandate, he was appointed to reside at Chongning Chan Temple and promoted to the rank of Sengtong (Head of the Sangha).

Seizing this opportunity, I fortunately sent a letter from afar to urge him on regarding his delay. Subsequently, Yongbong suddenly dispatched a monk to Mount Taepyeong to transcribe a Song-dynasty printed edition to serve as a copy.
Furthermore, he informed me that the original treasure transmitted within the Hwansil chamber of the Master of Mount Taepyeong had been lost.
The original manuscript has not yet arrived. I have merely sent this letter, saying:
"If this record reaches you today, your long-cherished hope will be fulfilled and my own wish will likewise be satisfied. Now, I trouble you once more:

you should commission a skilled calligrapher to transcribe it again from the printed copy and entrust it to a carver. Record the history of this record’s appearance and disappearance in the final pages.
Thus it has been bequeathed for future generations. Today, my long-cherished vow has finally been fulfilled. I reverently burn incense and read this work;
though eight hundred years have passed since the Great Master, he appears as if before my very eyes, no different from being face-to-face. How marvelous is this record!
It has not been seen in China for so long, yet that it is now published here in this land is a great fortune, indeed a most extraordinary blessing.
This is why I have composed this postscript, entrusting my humble intentions to future worthies.
Now, since our original teacher, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, took the trichiliocosm as his field of conversion, those who follow after him must likewise not forget his family precepts.
I have carefully observed the virtuous predecessors of India and China, who did not shrink from [the journey of] one hundred thousand [yojanas].
Traveling from west to east, they underwent hardships one after another, never shrinking from the loss of body or life.

Their resolve was not for profit, nor was it for fame; they merely upheld the model of their Master and transmitted the Dharma throughout the *sahasra-loka-dhātu*, delivering sentient beings across the boundless realms. As for the way they settled their minds, how could it be like that of today?

Those who falsely assume the guise of a "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra) harbor malice toward the inexhaustible brilliance of hundreds of thousands of lamps, while cherishing the single lamp of their own home in its dimness; they find delight in plundering others' clothing and food.
Furthermore, as for the Dharma studied by the followers of Chan and the Teachings in this land today, although it is fundamentally the Dharma of our Master, the Śākya Tathāgata of India—

Furthermore, as these teachings were transmitted to this land, all of them originated from China; thus, they serve to supplement what was omitted and fill what was deficient in the Chan and doctrinal traditions of China.
For those within the monastic community here, it is their duty to uphold the laws and precepts bequeathed by our Original Teacher.
This is what is called the way of reciprocity. Therefore, the deficiency in the scriptural traditions of the teachings of Zhendan (China) was preserved thanks to this land [of India].

Its traces shine upon the ancient records: formerly, Zhendan lost the *Nanyue Zhiguan* (The Stopping and Contemplation of Mount Nanyue), yet in the third year of the Xianping era of the Song dynasty, the Dharma Master Jizhao of this land brought the *Mahāyāna Śamatha-vipaśyanā* into Song. And...
The teachings and contemplations of Tiantai had declined and were restored to their full perfection.

Therefore, the Great Master Ciyun, the abbot of Tianzhu Monastery in Hangzhou during the Song dynasty, wrote the Postscript to the *Zhi Guan* (Calming and Contemplation), stating: "How magnificent is this Dharma! It first came from the West."
It is like the rising of the moon; now it returns once more to the east. It is like the ascent of the sun; its pure radiance and full brilliance shall circulate throughout our land.

Alas! How might this record be brought back again to Zhendan? May there be one in the Chan groves of Zhendan who, like Ciyun, can compose a postscript for later generations to elucidate the hidden and manifest aspects of this record’s cyclical circulation, alongside the *Biographies of the Meditation and Contemplation of Mount Nanyue*.
How lamentable! Today, as we carve this record, not a single character has been added to or subtracted from the Song edition print.
Although the names of those who assisted in the carving are recorded so that their labor is not lost, why is the śramaṇa Yicheng of Qianguangwang Temple alone omitted?
It is because Yicheng... [revised the text] before and after, consolidating it into a single volume of seventeen folios, yet he did not have his name carved. Indeed, Yicheng...

As for those whose study of the principles has not yet reached the profound depths of the scriptures, if they venture to debate the teachings of the patriarchs, their erroneous interpretations need not even be refuted.
The Venerable Jiyin of the Song dynasty once inscribed a preface to this record, stating:

"When Sun Gong Jue Xinglao, Director of the Right Censorate and a member of the Jixian Academy, was serving as Governor of Fuzhou, he commissioned a monk to compile this record. Scholars [regard] Jue..."

His achievement in awakening to the fundamental tenets was truly magnificent. My sole regret is that at the end of his compilation, he appended the words of the śramaṇa Yìchéng of Qiānguāngwáng Temple, who had re-edited the "Three Phrases" and "Four Capacities.
Yìchéng himself had not even seen the original text, yet he criticized others with such bias (and so forth).
This confirms the words of Jìyīn: for the Dharma-preaching of the Chan school is what is known through realized wisdom, and it is... great.

This is different from what can be measured by mere intellectual interpretation. Therefore, I have alone eliminated the erroneous interpretations of Yicheng, resolving the lingering regrets of Jiyin today and blocking the divergent paths for future students.
I shall transmit nothing but the true essence of the Great Master’s preaching of the Dharma. Although the Great Master’s preaching is transmitted in ink and paper today, it remains as if—
The excellent medicine retained by the skilled physician remains complete in its color, fragrance, and flavor, with none of its qualities lost.

For those with the karmic affinity to take it, there is no illness that will not be cured. Yet, some may mistakenly consume the poisonous medicine of Māra; struck by Māra’s poison, the toxic vapors penetrate deeply, causing their minds to become inverted.
They claim to have attained what they have not attained, and claim to have realized what they have not realized. Although the medicine has been given to them...
If they are unwilling to accept it, then even this record can do nothing for such people as these. Written with reverence by the old man Genkō of Dokuan on Mount Kyō,
on the twenty-first day of the eleventh month of the Gengwu year of the Genroku era,
at the Wōun-shitsu (Cloud-Reclining Chamber) of Ryūkō Seisha (Dragon Light Hermitage).
